ch53.anchor: did not even shave his pate
ch53.note: A samurai kept the front of his head shaved, the sakayaki, as a matter of daily grooming; to let it grow out was a visible sign of penance and withdrawal from affairs, like a Westerner going unshaven in mourning. Yoshinobu, having surrendered the government and shut himself in a sub-temple of the Kanei-ji at Ueno, wore the unshaven look of a man doing penance, the outward form of the “absolute submission” by which he hoped to spare Edo.

ch53.anchor: the Shōgitai was coming into being
ch53.note: The Shōgitai (“Corps to Manifest Righteousness”) was a body of pro-Tokugawa loyalists, many of them shogunal retainers, formed in Edo in early 1868 to resist the surrender their own lord had accepted. They took up position around Yoshinobu at Ueno; in the fifth month of that year the new government destroyed them in a single day’s bombardment, the Battle of Ueno. Their rise here marks how far events had slipped past Yoshinobu’s control.

These were the men who saved Edo. Katsu Kaishū, the shogunate’s naval commissioner, and Yamaoka Tesshū, a swordsman and envoy, negotiated with the new government’s commander Saigō Takamori and brought about the bloodless surrender of Edo Castle that spring, sparing the city the assault fixed for the fifteenth. Shiba passes on the theory, a plausible one, that it was Katsu who contrived to arm the Shinsengumi and send it off to Kōshū, precisely to be rid of the men whose presence in Edo most inflamed the Imperial side.

ch53.anchor: raise a monument to the two men
ch53.note: The monument is real and still stands: the Junsetsu Ryōyū no Hi (“Stone of the Two Heroes Martyred to Duty”) at Takahata Fudō in Hino. Every detail of Shiba’s aside is borne out: the inscription composed by the Sendai Confucian Ōtsuki Bankei, the calligraphy by Matsumoto Jun, the plan begun in the ninth year of Meiji (1876), the seal-script header written at last by Matsudaira Katamori after Yoshinobu could only weep at the names and refused, and the stone finally raised in 1888, held back a decade because a monument honoring men who died against the new government was slow to win permission. The weeping is the point the chapter has been building toward: even the lord who used and abandoned them could not, thirty years on, speak their names dry-eyed.

ch53.anchor: In Shimōsa (Chiba prefecture) it is a rich district
ch53.note: Nagareyama, on the Edo River in Shimōsa northeast of Edo, was a prosperous shogunal-domain town of brewers and merchants. Toshizō chooses it as a mustering ground on the road to the north; the reader who knows the history knows what he does not yet, that within weeks the Imperial columns will close on this camp, and that it is here the road of Kondō and Toshizō finally forks.

ch53.anchor: Aizu was still a powerful counter-force
ch53.note: Aizu (in today’s Fukushima), the domain of Matsudaira Katamori, the former Kyoto Protector, was the domain Satsuma and Chōshū hated above all others and the natural rallying-point of the north. It would become the core of the Northern Alliance and, that autumn, the scene of the war’s most terrible siege. Toshizō’s resolve to reach Aizu, formed here almost alone in the room, sets the course of everything that remains of his life, through the northern campaign to Hakodate.

ch53.anchor: the road I go out by—the spring moon
ch53.note: The verse is an actual hokku of Hijikata Toshizō’s, preserved in his manuscript collection under the poet-name Hōgyoku: kōyō ni / dete yuku michi ya / haru no tsuki, “setting out on official duty, the road, and the spring moon.” The cutting-word ya hangs the traveler between his errand and the moon above it. That he answers Kondō’s request for a poem with this one, on the eve of a last campaign, is the novelist’s quiet touch, not the historian’s.

As Kondō marches under the alias Ōkubo Yamato, Toshizō takes one of his own, Naitō Hayato, the name he will carry through the rest of the war. The two commanders of the disbanded Shinsengumi enter Nagareyama as shogunal officers no one there can name, which is exactly why the disguise will not hold once the Imperial scouts arrive.
